extracted.intended_audience: scientists, journal editors, peer reviewers, and research ethics committees (particularly in biomedical research)
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly commentary analysing limitations of the peer-review process illustrated by the Woo‑Suk Hwang stem‑cell fraud case and recommending practices (transparency, screening, centralisation, sanctions) to reduce fraud, plagiarism and double publication in scientific publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review as quality guardian, not integrity policeman
rubrics_metrics.description: The (anonymous) peer review process serves as goalkeeper of scientific quality rather than scientific integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers and editors can reasonably discriminate low- and high-quality papers but cannot reliably distinguish between good and excellent work; peer ratings have little predictive power for future citation. Therefore peer review should not be assumed to reliably detect intentional fabrication or criminal misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise reviewers' limited ability to detect fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers have no training in pursuing matters that turn out to be criminal and cannot be expected to act as policemen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reviewers are not trained crime investigators, burdening them with checking for fraud is unrealistic. Editorial systems should not rely solely on reviewers to uncover fabrication or serious misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralise and increase number of reviewers per manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralise the process of review and increase the number of reviewers per paper so more reviewers see each submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralisation would allow many more reviewers to assess a manuscript (two reviewers see more than one, three see more than two). This could improve detection of problems but requires structural change to the editorial system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access to reviewers' comments (post-publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attach reviewers' reports to manuscripts after publication (open access to reviewers' comments), with or without abandoning reviewer anonymity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing reviewer reports may improve transparency and review quality. Electronic publication removes page-limit obstacles. However, opening reviews may reduce reviewer willingness to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and manage tradeoffs of open review
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals advocating open review risk losing a substantial fraction of reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical survey (Cardiovascular Research) suggested a journal advocating revolutionary policy at the time would lose about 50% of its reviewers. Editors should weigh benefits of transparency against practical loss of reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plagiarism and duplicate-publication screening tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Programmes that can spot plagiarism and are used for screening students' papers should be used routinely by editors to detect plagiarism and autoplagiarism (double publications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screening tools are being optimised to compare strings across languages and are likely to become unavoidable tools for editors and possibly reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit undisclosed duplicate publication and require transparency for translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of substantially identical work in more than one place is misconduct; literal translations may be acceptable only if clearly identified as translations with reference to the original source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of near-identical twin papers (same data in Chinese and English journals) show this is a persistent problem. Editors should require disclosure and citation of previously published translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must check ethical provenance of materials/data
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical issues related to how data or biological materials were obtained (e.g., paid oocyte donors, lab members providing oocytes) should be assessed and can warrant rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unethical procurement should be handled by rejection of the manuscript and may be subject to prosecution under the offender's legal system; cultural differences may affect judgments but generally violation of accepted ethical standards should prevent publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate image/data irregularities (e.g., duplicated images, fabricated fingerprints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and journals should investigate and verify suspicious images and data (duplicated microscopic photographs, DNA fingerprint inconsistencies, fabricated karyotyping, teratoma photographs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hwang case demonstrated duplicated panels and identical DNA fingerprints where differences were expected; journals should request original data and, where necessary, commission independent investigation to verify authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and accessibility of investigation reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigation reports into alleged misconduct should be accessible rather than restricted to a few parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricted availability (e.g., translation accessible only to certain institutions) undermines trust. Greater openness about investigation findings helps the community understand failures in review and editorial oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility to respond and disclose reviewer reports when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should respond to serious post-publication concerns and consider disclosing reviewer reports or rationale for editorial decisions in misconduct cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note that Science did not provide original reviewers' reports upon request; silence from high-profile editors is unhelpful. Public editorials treating fraud as an accident rather than systemic issue are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider sanctions for proven fabrication (submission bans)
rubrics_metrics.description: When fabrication of data is involved, authors might be denied the right to submit manuscripts to scientific journals for a considerable period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejection may not be sufficient; stronger sanctions (temporary submission bans) could be considered to deter fabrication. Legal prosecution is separate and depends on jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish handling severity between ethical violations and fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation of ethical standards (e.g., unethical procurement) and fabrication of data are qualitatively different and may merit different responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although unethical procurement may be addressed by rejection (and possible legal action), fabrication is more dangerous and may warrant harsher sanctions. Care is required not to downplay fabrication's seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of systemic incentives that seduce misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization of modern science as a business — grant acquisition, publication, citation metrics — creates pressures that may seduce researchers into misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addressing misconduct requires acknowledging systemic incentives and career pressures; reviewers' goodwill ('good faith') may not be sufficient in this environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case studies of misconduct to improve review procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying high-profile fraud cases (e.g., Woo‑Suk Hwang) can reveal weaknesses in review and editorial processes and suggest reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical analysis of such cases highlights where concerns raised during review failed to prompt more scrutiny; lessons learned should inform policy changes (centralisation, transparency, screening).
